The Brahma Sūtras discuss the concept of avidyā (nescience) in relation to Brahman.
The Brahma Sūtras systematically discuss the nature of Brahman as the ultimate reality.

Madhva's Bhāṣya on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad from the Dvaita perspective, maintaining the eternal distinction (bheda) between the independent (svatantra) Viṣṇu and the dependent (paratantra) jīvas and matter; the neti-neti negates the world's independence, not its reality as Viṣṇu's creation.

Nimbārka's commentary tradition on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad from the Bhedābheda (Dvaitādvaita) perspective, teaching the simultaneous difference and non-difference of the jīva and Brahman, with Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa as the supreme couple.

Rāmānuja's Bhāṣya on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad from the Viśiṣṭādvaita perspective, interpreting the neti-neti as denying upādhi (limiting adjuncts) not Brahman's attributes, and emphasizing the qualified non-duality of Brahman with cit and acit.
Śaṅkara's Bhāṣya on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, the largest and one of the principal Upaniṣads, covering the madhu-vidyā, the yājñavalkya-maitreyī dialogue, and the neti-neti teaching.

Vallabha's Bhāṣya on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad from the Śuddhādvaita perspective, emphasizing the pure non-duality of Kṛṣṇa as Brahman, the world as His real manifestation (not māyā), and the path of puṣṭi-mārga (grace) through Kṛṣṇa-bhakti.
The Bṛhadīśvara Temple at Thanjavur is associated with Lord Shiva as its presiding deity.
The Bṛhadīśvara Temple celebrates Mahāśivarātri as a major festival.

Madhva's Bhāṣya on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, interpreting tat tvam asi as "you are that (servant of Viṣṇu)" — the jīva is a distinct reflection (pratibimba) of Viṣṇu, never identical; the sat-vidyā establishes Viṣṇu as the only independent reality.

Rāmānuja's Bhāṣya on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, interpreting tat tvam asi as the identity of the individual self (jīva) as a mode (prakāra) of Brahman, not absolute identity; the sat-vidyā as establishing Viṣṇu as the supreme Brahman qualified by the world.
Śaṅkara's Bhāṣya on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, famous for the sat-vidyā (being), the uddālaka-śvetaketu dialogue (tat tvam asi), and the dahara-vidyā (heart-space).

Madhva's Bhāṣya on the Taittirīya Upaniṣad, interpreting the five kośas as real gradations of being under Viṣṇu's control, the ānanda-mīmāṃsā as establishing hierarchical bliss, and the bhṛgu-vallī as the jīva's progressive service to Viṣṇu.

Rāmānuja's Bhāṣya on the Taittirīya Upaniṣad, interpreting the five kośas as real attributes of Brahman, the ānanda-mīmāṃsā as establishing graded bliss in Brahman's manifestations, and the bhṛgu-vallī as the progressive realization of Viṣṇu as the supreme.
Śaṅkara's Bhāṣya on the Taittirīya Upaniṣad, structured in three vallīs (śikṣā, brahmānanda, bhṛgu), teaching the five sheaths (pañca-kośa) and the ānanda-mīmāṃsā.
